The Scientific Revolution. The Scientific Revolution was the sixteenth- to eighteenth-century intellectual movement that fundamentally transformed how humans understood the natural world, replacing medieval authority with observation, experiment, and mathematical reasoning. Figures like Copernicus, Galileo, Descartes, and Newton overthrew ancient Greek certainties and the Church's cosmology, establishing the empirical method as the foundation of natural knowledge. This epoch marked the birth of modern science and laid the groundwork for the Enlightenment's faith in reason.

Copernicus displaced Earth from the center of the universe, proposing a heliocentric solar system that shattered medieval cosmology. Galileo used the telescope to observe moons orbiting Jupiter, providing direct evidence against the Earth-centered model and championing observation over received doctrine. René Descartes formalized the method of radical doubt through "I think, therefore I am" and mathematics as the language of nature, bridging philosophy and physics. Isaac Newton unified the heavens and Earth with his laws of motion and universal gravitation, creating a mechanistic cosmos governed by mathematics.

The printing press enabled rapid dissemination of new findings, creating networks of scientists across Europe who challenged authority collectively. Experimentation replaced mere authority. Knowledge claims required testable proof, not appeal to Aristotle or Church decree. The distinction between empiricism—knowledge from observation—and rationalism—knowledge from reason—emerged as both were needed for discovery. These thinkers connected to earlier humanist recovery of classical texts that provided mathematical and observational tools for scientific method. Together, they produced figures like the mathematician and philosopher Descartes, the astronomer and physicist Galileo, and the synthesizer Isaac Newton, who unified planetary motion and gravity into a unified mathematical system, ultimately establishing heliocentrism as the sun-centered model replacing Ptolemaic Earth-centrism.
